To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a novel dominant-negative mutation in ABCC8 (1508insAS) was found in three family members with severe CHI; 2) the mutation was present in both alleles in two affected family members and only in one allele in the healthy mother, and 3) this dominant-negative mutation affects the functional stoichimetry of the K(ATP) channel.
the clinical phenotype of congenital hyperisulinism is dependent on the relative expression of a mutated ABCC8 gene and that the methylation pattern of chromosome 11 is normal in this family.
the relative expression of the mutant ABCC8 allele in lymphocytes is the determinant for the clinical manifestation of a dominant mutation in ABCC8.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of the pathogenesis of CHI.
the genetic basis of the most common cause of severe hypoglycemia in infants, CHI.
the molecular mechanisms that cause congenital hyperinsulinaemia, and the clinical and genetic heterogeneity of this disorder.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the relative expression of the mutant and wild type alleles in the affected child and her aunt is responsible for their clinical phenotype, whereas their mothers, who express predominantly wild type, are asymptomatic.
the clinical phenotype of congenital hyperin-sulinism in this family is due to a dominant-negative effect of the 1507insAS mutation in ABCC8.
the clinical manifestation of CHI is determined by the relative expression of the mutant allele.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single base pair change in the ABCC8 gene can lead to a wide variety of clinical presentations of CHI, depending on the expression of the mutated allele.
a dominant-negative mutation in ABCC8 causes CHI.
the relative expression of a mutant ABCC8 allele in the presence of a normal allele determines the clinical phenotype of congenital hyperisulnism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of a mutated dominant ABCC8 allele is not necessarily associated with the severity of the disease, but rather, with the relative expression of the mutant allele.
the expression of a dominant mutant ABCC8 allele in a patient with CHI is not always associated with an increase in the mutant transcript level.
the relative expression of the mutant allele is a major determinant of the phenotype of CHI, even when the mutant allele is inherited in a maternal dominant pattern.
